rv.q: By treating horror as an art form rather than a cheap set of jump scares, this thrilling new show, which wears its connection to the world of the Paranormal Activity film franchise lightly, proves how jaw-clenchingly, arm-clutchingly frightening horror on stage can be.
A thrilling theatrical take on the horror movie franchise
If you enjoy the deliciously creepy feeling of your hair stirring on your tightening scalp in anticipation of terror, Paranormal Activity is the show for you.
In the best tradition of spooky theatre at this time of year, it sends you out huddling in your coat before you’ve even left the building.
Thoroughly exorcising the memory of that catastrophe, Paranormal Activity is about as good as stage horror gets.
Barrett leans fully into the live experience, and it pays off.
Paranormal Activity is not just a horror movie retread; it is a razor-sharp, immersive event that blends technical wizardry with genuine human dread.
The creative team have deployed their combined skills and talents to realise some genuinely creepy and unnerving moments which will surprise and please any fans of the horror genre.
Activity is not the scariest thing to grace the stage, there is a lot here that will leave audiences on tenterhooks.
Indeed, there’s a paint-by-numbers feel to much of the writing, not least as it pertains to these Americans’ view of London: the weather (tick), the food (huh?).
For others, it is a stylish but uneven attempt to translate cinematic terror into theatrical form.
In a city spoiled for theatrical hauntings, Paranormal Activity struggles to justify itself beyond brand recognition and a famous name above the title.
Horror should not be about thinking, it should be about feeling!
A pity, then, that the play proceeds at the pace of a snail, and there are one-hour plays out there that have more content than this two-hour one.
Paranormal Activity is, without a shadow of a doubt the best horror I have ever seen on stage, setting the gold standard for all others to follow.
Paranormal Activity: Live is properly, relentlessly frightening — arm-clutchingly, stranger-embracingly so.
It may not leave you afraid to turn off the lights at home, but in the moment, it delivers some genuinely effective shocks.
This is one for horror film buffs, and less so for theatre fans expecting a great play.

cn.t: Critics praise Paranormal Activity as genuinely terrifying theatre, with Felix Barrett's direction and Chris Fisher's illusions delivering visceral scares that justify the stage adaptation, though some find the story predictable and thin.

dr.inst: Rush tickets released at 10 AM via TodayTix app only. Until 25 April 2026.
